claims.claim: Counts may be truncated to {0,1,2} without losing any information relevant to level-3 restoration.
claims.evidence: For h(r)=min(2,r), h(a+b)=h(h(a)+h(b)) and h(ab)=h(h(a)h(b)) for all nonnegative integers. Thus h is a homomorphism to the saturated counting semiring. Matrix products therefore preserve exactly whether every relevant assignment count is zero, one, or at least two, which is precisely what the nested uniqueness predicates inspect.
claims.witness: The persisted checker tested both identities on 1,922 exact arithmetic cases and found no failure.
claims.search_method: Proved the two saturation identities by the cases zero, one, and at least two, then checked their use in each matrix-counting lift.

claims.claim: Level-3 additive restoration is decidable in O(m n^3) time under the source paper’s complexity convention.
claims.evidence: For fixed type-3 and type-2 values, the 2-by-2 matrix A counts type-1 column fillings by carry transition. Its product counts complete type-1 assignments. The 9-by-9 lift B then counts type-2 prefixes by their resulting saturated A-product state. Acceptance counts exactly those type-2 assignments having one type-1 completion, and outer reachability supplies the existential type-3 block. A column contains at most three variable cells, so enumeration across all local type-3, type-2, and type-1 tuples costs at most n^3; all lifted state factors are fixed constants. Over m columns this is O(m n^3) under the stated convention.
claims.witness: Direct quantifier evaluation and the lifted algorithm agreed on all 31,500 base-2 instances with one or two columns in the exhaustive checker.
claims.search_method: Re-derived both counting recurrences from the source quantifier order and accounted for every local digit loop and constant state factor.

claims.claim: Level-3 additive restoration is exactly a constant-state relational word problem after per-column normalization.
claims.evidence: The lifted state d lies in the fixed set {0,1,2}^9. For each normalized column, the relation d R_i e holds exactly when a local type-3 assignment produces e=dB_i(x). A global type-3 assignment induces such a path. Conversely, witnesses for successive edges combine because restoration variables in distinct columns are disjoint. The final-state predicate is exactly that one type-2 assignment has one type-1 completion with the required final carry.
claims.witness: The direct-versus-lifted exhaustive comparison covered every base-2 one- and two-column pattern over fixed 0, fixed 1, and types 1, 2, and 3.
claims.search_method: Checked both directions of the assignment/path correspondence, including initial carry, final carry, and disjointness of column variables.

claims.claim: The same construction places every fixed-level additive restoration problem in P.
claims.evidence: Inductively, eliminating a uniquely quantified digit type replaces a fixed N-state transition system by the saturated-count system {0,1,2}^N. For fixed level k, iterating this operation produces a finite state set depending only on k. The remaining outer existential block is layered reachability, while each column has only three cells and hence only polynomially many local assignments under the source convention.
claims.witness: The induction starts with the two carry states; each uniqueness block records a saturated distribution over the preceding fixed state set, and the outer block uses relations rather than another uniqueness lift.
claims.search_method: Induction on the fixed number of uniqueness quantifiers, separately verifying the existential outermost step.

claims.claim: Under the source paper’s polynomial-base convention and any uniform-AC0-decodable explicit-column encoding, every fixed-level additive restoration problem is in logspace-uniform NC1.
claims.evidence: For fixed k, the lifted state set is constant. Each bit of a column relation can be computed by constant-depth polynomial-size enumeration: candidate digits are guarded by digit<n; fixed-arity binary addition and comparison are uniform AC0; and saturated counts are represented by existence of one witness and existence of two distinct witnesses. The polynomial-base condition keeps these enumerations polynomial in input length. A balanced product tree for the resulting constant-dimensional Boolean relations has O(log N) depth and polynomial size. The assumed decoder and standard indexed construction give logspace uniformity.
claims.witness: A relation entry is reduced to fixed-depth Boolean combinations of explicit candidate assignments; no input-dependent state-space growth or unbounded quantifier depth remains.
claims.search_method: Expanded the local counting lifts into witness and distinct-witness predicates, then checked size, depth, bounded-fan-in conversion, and uniform generation of the balanced relation product.

claims.claim: Under the source paper’s polynomial encoding convention, every fixed-level additive restoration problem is decidable in deterministic logarithmic space; for every fixed base it is a regular column language.
claims.evidence: For fixed k, the current reachable-state bitset and all saturated tables have constant size. Local transitions can be recomputed with at most three O(log n)-bit digit counters plus an O(log m)-bit column counter. With n polynomially bounded in encoded length N, this is O(log N) workspace and polynomial time. When both level and base are fixed, the normalized column alphabet and state set are finite, and the reachable-set update, boundary carry, and acceptance condition form a finite automaton.
claims.witness: The logspace procedure scans or re-locates one explicit column at a time and never stores a digit assignment for more than its three cells.
claims.search_method: Performed a workspace accounting for counters, lifted states, parsing, and reachability; then specialized the normalized transition system to fixed base.

claims.claim: Level-3 additive restoration is formally P-complete under polynomial-time many-one reductions, but this does not provide the requested meaningful matching hardness classification.
claims.evidence: Membership in P follows from the verified algorithm. The language is nontrivial: in base 2 with required final carry zero, x_3+0=0 is satisfiable by x_3=0, whereas x_3+1=0 has no satisfying type-3 digit. For any language A in P, a polynomial-time decider for A can select between these two fixed instances, giving a polynomial-time many-one reduction. This vacuous reduction notion supplies no logspace or comparably discriminating hardness result.
claims.witness: Fixed YES instance: one column (T3,0,0), base 2, final carry 0. Fixed NO instance: one column (T3,1,0), base 2, final carry 0.
claims.search_method: Checked both fixed instances directly and applied the definition of polynomial-time many-one hardness.

claims.claim: Even in base 2 with no type-3 cells, level-3 additive restoration is ODD-PARITY-hard under constant-length projections, and therefore is not in AC0.
claims.evidence: Exact column enumeration gives A_U=[[2,1],[1,2]] and A_I as the identity. Starting from (1,0), U produces E=(2,1). Across VU, type-2 digit 0 maps (a,b) to (b,min(2,2b)), while digit 1 maps it to (min(2,2a),a). Hence E permits only 0 to reach O=(1,2), O permits only 1 to return to E, and every other choice reaches absorbing M=(2,2). The final-carry-zero count equals one exactly in O, so exactly one type-2 assignment is accepted precisely after an odd number of input ones. The two-column-per-bit mapping is a constant-length projection. Closure of AC0 under projections and the PARITY lower bound give nonmembership in AC0.
claims.witness: The checker verified all 8,191 bit words of lengths 0 through 12 using exact lifted transitions, with separate direct quantifier evaluation through length 3.
claims.search_method: Recomputed every gadget matrix from the base-2 column equation and exhaustively tested the resulting projection.

claims.claim: The meaningful classification is narrowed to a projection lower bound by ODD PARITY and a deterministic-logspace upper bound, but no matching hardness classification is established.
claims.evidence: Claims 5 and 7 establish ODD-PARITY hardness under projections and membership in deterministic logspace. Parity hardness only excludes AC0; it does not establish L-hardness or otherwise match the L upper bound. The draft explicitly refrains from claiming such a result.
claims.witness: The lower endpoint is witnessed by the U/I/V projection, while the upper endpoint is witnessed by the constant-state streaming algorithm.
claims.search_method: Compared the proved reduction strength and source class with the standard requirements for a matching completeness statement.

claims.claim: For uniform-AC0-decodable explicit-column encodings, the meaningful classification is narrowed to a projection lower bound by ODD PARITY and a logspace-uniform NC1 upper bound, but no matching hardness classification is established.
claims.evidence: Under the claim’s stated encoding and polynomial-base conditions, claim 4 supplies logspace-uniform NC1 membership and claim 7 supplies projection hardness for ODD PARITY. Projection hardness for one parity language is not NC1-hardness, and the draft gives no reduction from an NC1-complete language. Thus the stated bracket and its acknowledged gap are accurate.
claims.witness: The same explicit base-2 projection gives the lower endpoint; the balanced constant-relation product gives the conditional upper endpoint.
claims.search_method: Verified both endpoint arguments independently and checked that neither entails the missing NC1-hardness conclusion.

target_evidence: The draft proves substantial upper bounds—P for every fixed level, L under the source polynomial encoding convention, and encoding-qualified logspace-uniform NC1—plus an ODD-PARITY projection lower bound. Those bounds do not match: no L-hardness, NC1-hardness, or equivalent complete classification is proved. Because the exact source target requires both a complete upper bound and matching hardness classification, the target is not fully resolved. The parent labels its resolution PARTIAL and explicitly identifies this remaining gap, so that label is accurate rather than overstated.
